“There, he is not disliked; here, none tire of him. May he, morning and night, forever preserve his good repute to the end.”
Fei Shun

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭楊批周人忠厚之義發揮殆
盡深得詩正而葩之體錄之
考試官教諭周批詞理整贍佳文也
考試官教諭方批說譽字得旨而文亦可
觀取之
詩人於二代之後美其得人心於無間而保善
聲於無窮也蓋君子未有不得人心而蚤有譽
於天下者也今二代之後人心交愛寧有不保
其譽者乎此二王之後來助祭之詩也意謂德
===
之感於人者有廣狹之殊則譽之加於已者有
乆暫之異觀夫夏之後之為君於杞國也杞人
無小無大罔不愛之而有以愜一國之輿情殷
之後之為君於宋國也宋人無貴無賤靡不悅
之而有以慰一方之顯望其在彼無惡如此及
其服玆黼冓祼將于京也有嚴有翼而容貌脩
整自有以聳人之觀於薦廣牡相予肆祀也有
萋有且如澤鷺之潔白自有以快人之覩其在此
無斁又如此夫然則庶幾其能夙夜以永終
punctuated:
同考試官教諭楊批：「周人忠厚之義，發揮殆盡，深得詩正而葩之體，錄之。」
考試官教諭周批：「詞理整贍，佳文也。」
考試官教諭方批：「說譽字得旨，而文亦可觀，取之。」
詩人於二代之後，美其得人心於無間，而保善聲於無窮也。蓋君子未有不得人心而蚤有譽於天下者也。今二代之後，人心交愛，寧有不保其譽者乎？此二王之後來助祭之詩也。意謂德之感於人者有廣狹之殊，則譽之加於已者有乆暫之異。觀夫夏之後之為君於杞國也，杞人無小無大，罔不愛之，而有以愜一國之輿情；殷之後之為君於宋國也，宋人無貴無賤，靡不悅之，而有以慰一方之顯望。其在彼無惡如此。及其服玆黼冓，祼將于京也，有嚴有翼，而容貌脩整，自有以聳人之觀；於薦廣牡，相予肆祀也，有萋有且，如澤鷺之潔白，自有以快人之覩。其在此無斁又如此。夫然，則庶幾其能夙夜以永終
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “The meaning of the Zhou people’s loyalty and generosity is developed almost exhaustively. This profoundly captures the upright yet richly expressive character of the Poetry. Record it.”
Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: “The language and reasoning are orderly and ample. A fine essay.”
Examiner Fang, Instructor, comments: “The explanation of the word ‘reputation’ grasps the intended meaning, and the writing also merits attention. Accept it.”
The poet praises the descendants of the two dynasties for winning the people’s hearts without any estrangement and preserving their good name without end. For no gentleman has ever failed to win the people’s hearts yet gained an early reputation throughout the world. Now that the descendants of the two dynasties are universally loved, how could they fail to preserve their reputation? This is a poem about the descendants of the two royal houses coming to assist at the sacrifices. Its meaning is that, just as virtue varies in the breadth of its influence upon others, so the reputation bestowed upon oneself varies in its duration. Consider the descendant of Xia ruling the state of Qi: among the people of Qi, great and small alike, none fails to love him, and thus he satisfies the sentiments of the whole state. The descendant of Yin rules the state of Song: among the people of Song, noble and humble alike, none fails to delight in him, and thus he fulfills the manifest hopes of the region. Such is their being ‘without hatred there.’ When they wear these patterned ceremonial garments [?] and perform the libation in the capital, they are solemn and reverent, their appearance composed and orderly, naturally inspiring awe in those who behold them. When they present the great sacrificial bulls and ‘assist us in conducting the sacrifices,’ they are dignified and poised, as pure and white as egrets in a marsh, naturally delighting those who see them. Such, too, is their being ‘never wearisome here.’ This being so, one may hope that, early and late, they can forever preserve to the end…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
此譽矣蓋二君者天子有事膰焉有喪拜焉尊
威不同乎列國人固以此而稱之也統承先王
用天子禮樂尊寵大異乎庶邦人固以此而譽
之也然或不為人心之所歸則膰焉拜焉之禮
或有時而不然矣今既有以致人之交愛則足
以俾有周之無斁而今日之所稱者雖百歲猶
一日可也夙而復夜夜而復夙寧有不稱之時
耶或不為人心之所向則天子禮樂之用或有
時而中輟矣今既有以致人之胥悅則足以與
===
我國而咸休而今日之所譽者雖沒世而不渝
可也自夙而夜自夜而夙寧有失譽之時耶是
則人不難於保譽而難於得人心苟於其難者
而能易則夫易者又何難之有耶周王獻助祭
之臣而其言如此其愛人以德也何如哉大抵
興王之君必存二代之後者所以尊其先世受
命之君俾承祀而不廢且示天下公器又使時
君常以覆車為戒耳蓋一舉而眾義具焉此有
周之法之所以為善而非後世之所能及也
punctuated: 此譽矣。蓋二君者，天子有事膰焉，有喪拜焉，尊威不同乎列國，人固以此而稱之也。統承先王，用天子禮樂，尊寵大異乎庶邦，人固以此而譽之也。然或不為人心之所歸，則膰焉拜焉之禮，或有時而不然矣。今既有以致人之交愛，則足以俾有周之無斁，而今日之所稱者，雖百歲猶一日可也。夙而復夜，夜而復夙，寧有不稱之時耶？或不為人心之所向，則天子禮樂之用，或有時而中輟矣。今既有以致人之胥悅，則足以與我國而咸休，而今日之所譽者，雖沒世而不渝可也。自夙而夜，自夜而夙，寧有失譽之時耶？是則人不難於保譽，而難於得人心。苟於其難者而能易，則夫易者又何難之有耶？周王獻助祭之臣，而其言如此，其愛人以德也何如哉！大抵興王之君必存二代之後者，所以尊其先世受命之君，俾承祀而不廢，且示天下公器，又使時君常以覆車為戒耳。蓋一舉而眾義具焉，此有周之法之所以為善，而非後世之所能及也。
translation_en:
…this good name. For these two rulers, when the Son of Heaven conducts sacrifices, he sends them sacrificial meat; when they suffer a bereavement, he pays his respects. Their dignity and authority differ from those of the other states, and people naturally commend them for this. They continue the succession of the former kings and use the rites and music of the Son of Heaven. The honor and favor they enjoy greatly exceed those accorded to the other states, and people naturally praise them for this. Yet if people's hearts did not turn to them, the courtesies of sending sacrificial meat and paying respects at a bereavement might sometimes cease to be observed. Now that they have secured people's common affection, however, they can keep Zhou from ever tiring of them; the commendation they receive today may remain the same for a hundred years as for a single day. Morning follows evening, and evening follows morning: could there ever be a time when they were not commended? If people's hearts did not incline toward them, their use of the Son of Heaven's rites and music might sometimes be interrupted. Now that they have secured people's common delight, however, they can share in the blessings of our state; the praise they receive today may endure unchanged throughout their lives. From morning until evening, and from evening until morning: could there ever be a time when they lost their good name? Thus the difficulty lies not in preserving one's good name, but in winning people's hearts. If one can make the difficult part easy, what difficulty could the easy part present? The king of Zhou made an offering to the ministers assisting at the sacrifice [?], and his words were such as these. How deeply he loved others through virtue!

Generally, a ruler who establishes a royal dynasty invariably preserves the descendants of the two preceding dynasties. He thereby honors their ancestral rulers who received Heaven's Mandate and enables their sacrifices to continue without interruption. He also shows that All-under-Heaven is a public trust and makes the reigning ruler constantly heed the warning of an overturned carriage—the downfall of his predecessors. Thus a single action embodies many principles of righteousness. This is why Zhou's institutions were excellent, beyond what later ages could match.

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
此譽矣蓋二君者天子有事膰焉有喪拜焉尊
威不同乎列國人固以此而稱之也統承先王
用天子禮樂尊寵大異乎庶邦人固以此而譽
之也然或不為人心之所歸則膰焉拜焉之禮
或有時而不然矣今既有以致人之交愛則足
以俾有周之無斁而今日之所稱者雖百歲猶
一日可也夙而復夜夜而復夙寧有不稱之時
耶或不為人心之所向則天子禮樂之用或有
時而中輟矣今既有以致人之胥悅則足以與
===
我國而咸休而今日之所譽者雖沒世而不渝
可也自夙而夜自夜而夙寧有失譽之時耶是
則人不難於保譽而難於得人心苟於其難者
而能易則夫易者又何難之有耶周王獻助祭
之臣而其言如此其愛人以德也何如哉大抵
興王之君必存二代之後者所以尊其先世受
命之君俾承祀而不廢且示天下公器又使時
君常以覆車為戒耳蓋一舉而眾義具焉此有
周之法之所以為善而非後世之所能及也
punctuated: 此譽矣。蓋二君者，天子有事膰焉，有喪拜焉，尊威不同乎列國，人固以此而稱之也。統承先王，用天子禮樂，尊寵大異乎庶邦，人固以此而譽之也。然或不為人心之所歸，則膰焉拜焉之禮，或有時而不然矣。今既有以致人之交愛，則足以俾有周之無斁，而今日之所稱者，雖百歲猶一日可也。夙而復夜，夜而復夙，寧有不稱之時耶？或不為人心之所向，則天子禮樂之用，或有時而中輟矣。今既有以致人之胥悅，則足以與我國而咸休，而今日之所譽者，雖沒世而不渝可也。自夙而夜，自夜而夙，寧有失譽之時耶？是則人不難於保譽，而難於得人心。苟於其難者而能易，則夫易者又何難之有耶？周王獻助祭之臣，而其言如此，其愛人以德也何如哉！大抵興王之君，必存二代之後者，所以尊其先世受命之君，俾承祀而不廢，且示天下公器，又使時君常以覆車為戒耳。蓋一舉而眾義具焉，此有周之法之所以為善，而非後世之所能及也。
translation_en: …this praise. For these two rulers, when the Son of Heaven performs sacrifices, he sends them sacrificial meat; when they suffer bereavement, he bows to them. Their honor and dignity differ from those of the other states, and people certainly acclaim them for this. They inherit the succession of the former kings and use the rites and music of the Son of Heaven. The honor and favor they enjoy far exceed those of the other states, and people certainly praise them for this. Yet if people’s hearts do not turn to them, the rites of sending sacrificial meat and bowing to them may at times cease to be observed. Now that they have secured people’s mutual affection, they can ensure that Zhou never tires of them, and the acclaim they receive today may remain the same for a hundred years as for a single day. Morning gives way to night, and night again to morning: could there ever be a time when they are not acclaimed? If people’s hearts do not incline toward them, their use of the Son of Heaven’s rites and music may at times be interrupted. Now that they have secured the shared delight of the people, they can enjoy blessings together with our state, and the praise they receive today may remain unchanged to the end of their lives. From morning to night, and from night to morning: could there ever be a time when they lose their good repute? Thus the difficulty lies not in preserving a good reputation, but in winning people’s hearts. If they can make the difficult thing easy, what difficulty could there be in the easy thing? They also thereby show that All-under-Heaven is a public trust and cause the reigning ruler constantly to take the overturned chariot of his predecessors as a warning. Thus a single act embodies many principles of righteousness. This is why the institutions of Zhou were excellent, beyond what later ages could match.

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
春秋
初獻六羽隱公五年衛人來媵成公八年伯姬
歸于宋季孫行父如宋致女晉人
來媵俱成公九年齊人來媵成公十年
侯嘉祥

子率多舉此遺彼輕重失宜獨此作體悉明白又筆
力雄偉治經者顧不當爾耶是宜錄出
考試官教諭周批詞足以發經旨佳士也
===
考試官教諭方批得胡傳意
祀樂舉春秋因褒以見貶婚禮行春秋因貶以
見褒夫褒貶為春秋大法固有相因以見而不
可偏廢者也考諸魯事則聖心之公可知矣且
六羽之獻于魯也祀仲子於新宫損文樂之舊
數斯亦祀事之常耳何謂因褒以見貶耶蓋天
子八佾諸侯六佾此樂制也今舞列以六恪遵
周室之制度降殺以兩無復分外之僭踰斯可
褒矣然魯之所以頻僭差者果可得而掩哉是
punctuated:
春秋
初獻六羽，隱公五年；衛人來媵，成公八年；伯姬歸于宋，季孫行父如宋致女，晉人來媵，俱成公九年；齊人來媵，成公十年。
侯嘉祥
同考試官教諭陳批：題本傳中之冠冕者，士子率多舉此遺彼，輕重失宜。獨此作體悉明白，又筆力雄偉。治經者顧不當爾耶？是宜錄出。
考試官教諭周批：詞足以發經旨，佳士也。
考試官教諭方批：得胡傳意。
祀樂舉，《春秋》因褒以見貶；婚禮行，《春秋》因貶以見褒。夫褒貶為《春秋》大法，固有相因以見而不可偏廢者也。考諸魯事，則聖心之公可知矣。且六羽之獻于魯也，祀仲子於新宫，損文樂之舊數，斯亦祀事之常耳。何謂因褒以見貶耶？蓋天子八佾，諸侯六佾，此樂制也。今舞列以六，恪遵周室之制度；降殺以兩，無復分外之僭踰，斯可褒矣。然魯之所以頻僭差者，果可得而掩哉？是
translation_en:
Spring and Autumn Annals

“For the first time, six rows of feather dancers were presented”—the fifth year of Duke Yin. “Men of Wei came to escort accompanying brides”—the eighth year of Duke Cheng. “Bo Ji went to marry in Song”; “Jisun Xingfu went to Song to formally entrust the bride”; “Men of Jin came to escort accompanying brides”—all in the ninth year of Duke Cheng. “Men of Qi came to escort accompanying brides”—the tenth year of Duke Cheng.

Hou Jiaxiang

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: These topics are among the foremost in the commentary on this classic. Candidates generally address one point and omit another, giving improper weight to the various issues. This composition alone shows thorough and clear understanding, together with a powerful and imposing literary style. Should those who study the classics not indeed write thus? It deserves to be selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Zhou, Instructor: His language fully brings out the meaning of the classic. A fine scholar.

Comment by Examiner Fang, Instructor: He has grasped the meaning of Hu’s Commentary.

When sacrificial music is performed, the Spring and Autumn Annals conveys blame through praise; when marriage rites are conducted, it conveys praise through blame. Praise and blame constitute the great guiding principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals. There are indeed instances in which each is revealed through the other, and neither may be neglected. Examining the affairs of Lu makes the impartiality of the sage’s mind apparent.

Now, when six rows of feather dancers were presented in Lu, Zhongzi was being sacrificed to in the new temple. The former number of dancers in the civil dance was reduced: this was merely the normal observance of sacrificial ritual. Why, then, speak of conveying blame through praise? The Son of Heaven had eight rows of dancers, and the feudal lords six: this was the prescribed system for ritual music. To arrange the dancers now in six rows was scrupulously to follow the institutions of the Zhou royal house; to reduce their number by two rows meant that there was no longer any presumptuous encroachment beyond the allotted rank. This deserved praise. Yet could Lu’s repeated ritual usurpations and deviations really be concealed? This…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
故在大廟則用以祀周公非所以康周公也在
群廟則用以祀群公非所以尊群公也今日之
用六旣是則前此之用八果非矣春秋之法好
而知其惡特書初獻見魯之得不足以救旣往
之失固褒之也實貶之也若伯姬之歸于宋也
來媵則衛晉與齊致女則季孫行父斯亦婚姻
之常耳何謂因貶以見褒耶蓋諸侯一娶九女
大夫承命往致此禮制也今三國來媵則縱欲
之罪有歸貴卿遣行則溺愛之私以著斯宜貶
===
矣然伯姬之所以特取重者豈無自而然哉是
故賢行著於家故致女使卿特厚其嫁遣之禮
賢名聞於遠故諸國爭媵信其無妬忌之行內
外之逾制雖非而伯姬之賢德不誣矣春秋之
法惡而知其美據事詳書見在人之失不能以
掩伯姬之賢固貶之也亦褒之也噫貶不以褒
而廢則人知惡之當戒褒不以貶而廢則人知
善之當勉聖人之心何心哉大抵善惡者在人
之情褒貶者天下之公聖人心無毀譽如鏡之
punctuated:
故在大廟，則用以祀周公，非所以康周公也；在群廟，則用以祀群公，非所以尊群公也。今日之用六旣是，則前此之用八果非矣。《春秋》之法，好而知其惡，特書「初獻」，見魯之得不足以救旣往之失。固褒之也，實貶之也。
若伯姬之歸于宋也，來媵則衛、晉與齊，致女則季孫行父，斯亦婚姻之常耳。何謂因貶以見褒耶？蓋諸侯一娶九女，大夫承命往致，此禮制也。今三國來媵，則縱欲之罪有歸；貴卿遣行，則溺愛之私以著。斯宜貶矣。然伯姬之所以特取重者，豈無自而然哉？是故賢行著於家，故致女使卿，特厚其嫁遣之禮；賢名聞於遠，故諸國爭媵，信其無妬忌之行。內外之逾制雖非，而伯姬之賢德不誣矣。《春秋》之法，惡而知其美，據事詳書，見在人之失不能以掩伯姬之賢。固貶之也，亦褒之也。
噫！貶不以褒而廢，則人知惡之當戒；褒不以貶而廢，則人知善之當勉。聖人之心何心哉？大抵善惡者，在人之情；褒貶者，天下之公。聖人心無毀譽，如鏡之
translation_en:
… Thus, in the Grand Ancestral Temple, they used it to sacrifice to the Duke of Zhou, but this was no way to bring peace to the Duke of Zhou; in the other ancestral temples, they used it to sacrifice to the other dukes, but this was no way to honor those dukes. If using six ranks of dancers now was correct, then their earlier use of eight was indeed wrong. The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals is to recognize faults even in what it approves. It specifically records the “first presentation,” showing that Lu’s correct action could not make good its past errors. Certainly this is praise, yet in substance it is censure.
As for Bo Ji’s marriage into Song, Wei, Jin, and Qi sent accompanying brides, while Jisun Hangfu formally presented the bride. These, too, were merely customary marriage arrangements. Why say that censure serves to reveal praise? Under the ritual regulations, a feudal lord received nine women in a single marriage, and a grand master was commissioned to go and formally present the bride. Here, however, three states sent accompanying brides, so responsibility for indulging desire could be assigned; and a high minister was dispatched, revealing the partiality of excessive affection. These things deserved censure. Yet could the exceptional esteem accorded Bo Ji have been without cause? Her virtuous conduct was manifest at home, so a minister was sent to present her, making the ceremonies for her marriage and departure especially lavish. Her reputation for virtue was known far away, so the various states competed to send accompanying brides, trusting that she would display no jealousy. Although the departures from prescribed forms both at home and abroad were wrong, Bo Ji’s virtue was beyond dispute. The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals is to recognize merits even in what it condemns. It records the events in detail according to the facts, showing that the faults of others could not obscure Bo Ji’s virtue. Certainly this is censure, but it is also praise.
Ah! When censure is not abandoned because of praise, people know that they must guard against evil; when praise is not abandoned because of censure, people know that they must strive toward goodness. What kind of mind is the sage’s mind? In general, goodness and evil belong to human dispositions, while praise and censure constitute the impartial judgment of all under Heaven. The sage’s mind harbors neither disparagement nor acclaim, like a mirror’s …

故在大廟，則用以祀周公，非所以康周公也；在群廟，則用以祀群公，非所以尊群公也。今日之用六旣是，則前此之用八果非矣。春秋之法，好而知其惡，特書「初獻」，見魯之得不足以救旣往之失，固褒之也，實貶之也。
若伯姬之歸于宋也，來媵則衛、晉與齊，致女則季孫行父，斯亦婚姻之常耳，何謂因貶以見褒耶？蓋諸侯一娶九女，大夫承命往致，此禮制也。今三國來媵，則縱欲之罪有歸；貴卿遣行，則溺愛之私以著。斯宜貶矣。然伯姬之所以特取重者，豈無自而然哉？是故賢行著於家，故致女使卿，特厚其嫁遣之禮；賢名聞於遠，故諸國爭媵，信其無妬忌之行。內外之逾制雖非，而伯姬之賢德不誣矣。春秋之法，惡而知其美，據事詳書，見在人之失不能以掩伯姬之賢，固貶之也，亦褒之也。
噫！貶不以褒而廢，則人知惡之當戒；褒不以貶而廢，則人知善之當勉。聖人之心何心哉？大抵善惡者，在人之情；褒貶者，天下之公。聖人心無毁譽，如鏡之
translation_en:
…Thus, in the Grand Ancestral Temple, it was used to sacrifice to the Duke of Zhou, but was no means of bringing repose to the Duke of Zhou [?]; in the other ancestral temples, it was used to sacrifice to the other dukes, but was no means of honoring them. If using six ranks of dancers on this occasion was right, then the earlier use of eight was indeed wrong. The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals is to recognize faults even in what it approves. By expressly recording the “first presentation,” it shows that Lu’s correct action could not remedy its past errors. Certainly this conveys praise, but in fact it also conveys blame.
As for Bo Ji’s marriage into Song, Wei, Jin, and Qi sent accompanying brides, while Jisun Hangfu formally delivered the bride. These were merely customary matters of marriage: why say that blame here serves to reveal praise? A feudal lord takes nine women in a single marriage, and a grand master receives orders to go and formally deliver the bride: this is the ritual rule. Here, however, three states sent accompanying brides, so responsibility for indulging desire had someone to fall upon; a high-ranking minister was dispatched, thereby exposing the partiality of excessive affection. This certainly deserved blame. Yet could there have been no reason why Bo Ji was held in such exceptional esteem? Her virtuous conduct was manifest at home; hence a minister was sent to deliver her, making the ceremonial arrangements for her marriage and departure exceptionally generous. Her reputation for virtue was known far away; hence the states competed to send accompanying brides, trusting that her conduct was free of jealousy. Although the departures from the rules both at home and abroad were wrong, Bo Ji’s virtuous character was no fabrication. The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals is to recognize merits even in what it condemns. By recording the circumstances in detail as they occurred, it shows that the faults of others could not obscure Bo Ji’s virtue. Certainly this conveys blame, but it also conveys praise.
Ah! When blame is not set aside on account of praise, people know that they must guard against evil; when praise is not set aside on account of blame, people know that they must strive toward goodness. What kind of mind does the Sage possess? In general, goodness and evil belong to human dispositions, while praise and blame express the impartial judgment of all under Heaven. The Sage’s mind contains neither disparagement nor commendation, just as a mirror…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
無妍醜也因事物善惡而施褒貶焉不期公而
自公耳然則有天下國家之責而司賞罰之權
者亦何莫學夫春秋
齊師遷紀郱郼郚莊公九年
拱廷臣
同考試官教諭陳批聖經言師言遷傳有明
據此作乃能發文定意於千載之上可謂得謹嚴之法
者高薦何忝
考試官教諭周批發揮傳意不混不遺傑
===
作也允宜高薦
考試官教諭方批非精於治經者不能有
此錄之
春秋於大國遷邑顯其迫小之强著其滅小之
罪此郱郼郚之徙所以變文言師言遷也在昔
紀以蕞爾之邦密邇齊人之境啟釁積忿乆已
成於世讎動衆構兵近又增乎新怨至乃大舉
一國之衆而為三邑之遷使其民不獲享安土
之利致其君不能庇重遷之民紀之受禍亦云
punctuated:
無妍醜也，因事物善惡而施褒貶焉，不期公而自公耳。然則有天下國家之責而司賞罰之權者，亦何莫學夫《春秋》？

齊師遷紀郱郼郚。莊公九年。
拱廷臣。

同考試官教諭陳批：聖經言師言遷，傳有明據。此作乃能發文定意於千載之上，可謂得謹嚴之法者，高薦何忝？

考試官教諭周批：發揮傳意，不混不遺，傑作也，允宜高薦。

考試官教諭方批：非精於治經者不能有此，錄之。

《春秋》於大國遷邑，顯其迫小之强，著其滅小之罪。此郱郼郚之徙，所以變文言師言遷也。在昔，紀以蕞爾之邦，密邇齊人之境，啟釁積忿，乆已成於世讎；動衆構兵，近又增乎新怨。至乃大舉一國之衆，而為三邑之遷，使其民不獲享安土之利，致其君不能庇重遷之民。紀之受禍，亦云
translation_en:
…has neither beauty nor ugliness of its own. It accords praise and blame according to the good and evil in affairs and things; without aiming at impartiality, it is impartial of itself. Should not those responsible for the realm and its states and families, who wield the authority to reward and punish, likewise take the Spring and Autumn Annals as their model?

“The army of Qi relocated Ji’s towns of Ping, Yi [?], and Wu.” Ninth year of Duke Zhuang.
By Gong Tingchen.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: “The sage’s classic says ‘army’ and ‘relocated’; the commentary provides clear grounds for this wording. This composition brings to light the meaning of Wending [Hu Anguo], reaching back across a thousand years. It may be said to have grasped the method of meticulous precision and strict judgment. How could a high recommendation be undeserved?”

Comment by Examiner Zhou, Instructor: “It develops the commentary’s meaning without confusion or omission. A masterful composition, fully deserving a high recommendation.”

Comment by Examiner Fang, Instructor: “Only someone accomplished in the study of the classics could produce this. Accept it.”

When the Spring and Autumn Annals records a great state relocating towns, it exposes the force with which that state oppresses a smaller one and makes manifest its guilt in destroying it. This is why, in recording the removal of Ping, Yi [?], and Wu, it varies its wording to say ‘army’ and ‘relocated.’ In earlier times, Ji, a tiny state, lay immediately beside Qi’s territory. Provocations and accumulated resentment had long since developed into a hereditary feud; mobilizing troops and undertaking warfare had lately added fresh grievances. Matters reached the point where Qi mobilized the forces of its entire state to relocate the three towns. It prevented their people from enjoying the benefits of dwelling securely on their own land and left their ruler unable to protect his people, who were loath to leave their homes. The calamity suffered by Ji could indeed be called…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
惜矣齊之肆惡亦已甚矣聖人脩經至此有槩
于中故遷不言師而特以師稱者若曰為國圖
存紀之力猶足與守大衆見迫齊之勢莫之敢
當干戈是加驅之為已屬也戎馬是蹂攘之為
已利也噫籲衆感出矢言盤庚之所以安衆志
者果無謂哉顧乃憑其横逆脅使降附彊凌弱
衆暴寡非甚不義者為之乎故特稱師見紀畏
威而遷齊之暴因一言而顯矣夫邑不言遷而
特以遷書者若曰三邑之遷固于斯而不免紀
===
國之亡亦自此而莫支其貪若狼盡疆其土地
矣其食如蠶盡有其人民矣噫興滅國繼絕世
武王之所以歸民心者豈無道哉顧乃恣行殄
滅殘忍無忌弱之肉強之食非至不仁者為之
乎故特書遷見紀自是而滅齊之罪不再貶而
見矣吁必稱師而後齊之暴顯必書遷而後齊
之罪著謂春秋為孔子之刑書信矣夫抑猶有
說焉齊為無道暴虐乎紀為紀計者正宜早為
善圖求以免禍可也夫何前日憤然與戰大非
punctuated:
惜矣！齊之肆惡亦已甚矣！聖人脩經至此，有槩于中。故遷不言師，而特以師稱者，若曰：為國圖存，紀之力猶足與守；大衆見迫，齊之勢莫之敢當。干戈是加，驅之為已屬也；戎馬是蹂，攘之為已利也。噫！籲衆感，出矢言，盤庚之所以安衆志者，果無謂哉？顧乃憑其横逆，脅使降附，彊凌弱，衆暴寡，非甚不義者為之乎？故特稱師，見紀畏威而遷，齊之暴因一言而顯矣。夫邑不言遷，而特以遷書者，若曰：三邑之遷，固于斯而不免；紀國之亡，亦自此而莫支。其貪若狼，盡疆其土地矣；其食如蠶，盡有其人民矣。噫！興滅國，繼絕世，武王之所以歸民心者，豈無道哉？顧乃恣行殄滅，殘忍無忌，弱之肉，強之食，非至不仁者為之乎？故特書遷，見紀自是而滅，齊之罪不再貶而見矣。吁！必稱師而後齊之暴顯，必書遷而後齊之罪著，謂《春秋》為孔子之刑書，信矣夫！

抑猶有說焉：齊為無道，暴虐乎紀，為紀計者，正宜早為善圖，求以免禍可也。夫何前日憤然與戰，大非
translation_en:
…lamentable indeed! Qi’s unrestrained wickedness had also gone much too far! When the Sage reached this point in revising the classic, indignation stirred within him. Ordinarily, an entry recording a removal does not mention an army; here, however, an army is expressly named. It is as though the text were saying: in seeking to preserve their state, the people of Ji still had sufficient strength to defend it; but when pressed by a great host, none dared withstand Qi’s might. Qi brought weapons against them, driving them into subjection to itself; its warhorses trampled them, seizing them for its own advantage. Ah! Pan Geng called out to the distressed multitude [?] and issued solemn declarations: was his means of steadying the people’s resolve really without purpose? Yet Qi relied on its overbearing violence to force them into submission and allegiance. The strong oppressed the weak, and the many brutalized the few. Could anyone but the profoundly unrighteous have done this? Thus the text expressly names an “army,” showing that Ji removed its people out of fear of military force. Through this single word, Qi’s brutality is exposed.

Ordinarily, towns are not said to be “removed”; here, however, “removed” is expressly written. It is as though the text were saying: the removal of the three towns had now become unavoidable, and from this point onward the fall of the state of Ji could no longer be averted. Wolfishly greedy, Qi incorporated all Ji’s lands into its own territory; devouring like a silkworm, it took possession of all Ji’s people. Ah! King Wu restored extinguished states and continued severed lines of succession, thereby winning the people’s allegiance. Was there no moral principle in this? Yet Qi recklessly pursued annihilation, cruel and without restraint: the flesh of the weak became food for the strong. Could anyone but the utterly inhumane have done this? Thus the text expressly writes “removed,” showing that Ji’s extinction proceeded from this point. Qi’s guilt is apparent without any further condemnation. Alas! Only by naming the “army” is Qi’s brutality exposed; only by writing “removed” is Qi’s guilt made manifest. How true it is to call the Spring and Autumn Annals Kongzi’s book of punishments!

Yet there is something further to say. Qi acted without the Way and treated Ji with violence and cruelty. Those planning on Ji’s behalf ought surely to have devised a sound strategy early, seeking thereby to avert disaster. Why, then, had they previously fought Qi in anger, greatly at odds with…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
保邦之道頻年主魯求援又非可宗之人速國
之亡也固亦宜矣若夫齊襄隱忍於朝紀優容
於存季矯勉於葬伯姬逆天悖理無所不為乃
欲以是為禮為義為仁以蓋其滅國之惡吾誰
欺欺天乎
禮記
天垂象聖人則之郊所以明天道也
蔣識
同考試官教諭林批則天象明天道處惟此
===
篇能說出人所未說細玩之深有意味予必有所受之
也宜錄之以定初學禮者不決之議
考試官教諭周批得經旨
考試官教諭方批有考據
記者原取法於天之由著大報於天之義夫聖
人則天之象者則天之道也饗帝於郊而大報
之非明天之道而何哉昔記者論郊及此謂夫
報以功施有是功則有是祭禮以義起有是祭
則有是義盍於郊而觀之是故日月者天垂之
punctuated:
保邦之道。頻年主魯求援，又非可宗之人，速國之亡也，固亦宜矣。若夫齊襄隱忍於朝紀，優容於存季，矯勉於葬伯姬，逆天悖理，無所不為，乃欲以是為禮、為義、為仁，以蓋其滅國之惡，吾誰欺？欺天乎？

禮記
天垂象，聖人則之。郊，所以明天道也。
蔣識

考試官教諭周批：得經旨。
考試官教諭方批：有考據。

記者原取法於天之由，著大報於天之義。夫聖人則天之象者，則天之道也。饗帝於郊而大報之，非明天之道而何哉？昔記者論郊及此，謂夫報以功施，有是功則有是祭；禮以義起，有是祭則有是義。盍於郊而觀之？是故日月者，天垂之
translation_en:
…the way to preserve a state. Year after year, Ji relied on Lu and sought its aid; yet this, too, was no worthy leader to follow. It was therefore only to be expected that Ji should hasten its own destruction. As for Duke Xiang of Qi, he exercised restraint when receiving Ji at court [?], showed forbearance in allowing Ji Ji to remain, and forced himself to make an effort over Bo Ji’s burial. He defied Heaven and violated principle, stopping at nothing; yet he wished to present these acts as ritual propriety, righteousness, and benevolence, thereby concealing the evil of his destruction of a state. “Whom am I deceiving? Am I deceiving Heaven?”

Book of Rites
“Heaven displays its images, and the sage takes them as his model. The suburban sacrifice is the means of making manifest the Way of Heaven.”
Jiang Shi 蔣識

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: In explaining how the sage models himself on Heaven’s images and makes manifest Heaven’s Way, this essay alone says what others have not said. Careful reflection reveals profound significance. I must have received some instruction from it [?]. It should be included to settle questions that remain unresolved among those beginning the study of ritual.
Comment by Examiner Zhou, Instructor: Grasps the meaning of the classic.
Comment by Examiner Fang, Instructor: Supported by textual evidence.

The compiler of the Record traces the reason for taking Heaven as a model and sets forth the meaning of the great requital offered to Heaven. When the sage takes Heaven’s images as his model, he is taking Heaven’s Way as his model. To offer sacrifice to the Lord on High in the suburbs and thereby make the great requital—what is this if not making manifest Heaven’s Way? When the compiler discussed the suburban sacrifice and reached this point, his meaning was that requital responds to meritorious beneficence: where there is such beneficence, there is a corresponding sacrifice. Ritual arises from righteousness: where there is such a sacrifice, there is a corresponding moral justification. Why not examine this in the suburban sacrifice? Thus, the sun and moon are what Heaven displays…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
象也聖人于以動而觀靜而玩萬事之紀立焉
星辰者天垂之象也聖人于以遠而探近而索
四時之柄定焉如日中星鳥日永星火東作南
訛之事斯興其他開一務成一物何者不本於
天象以為之考中度衷乎宵中星虛日短星昴
西成朔易之事斯舉其他創一法立一制何者
不本諸天象以為之利用厚生乎然作則雖始
於聖人垂象實原於天道先王於是時維冬至
罄對越之忱禋於南郊之丘以冕則異於常也
===
以裘則異於常也日用上辛竭奏格之精禋於
南郊之兆以車則異於常也以旗則異於常也
是非徼福以自媚也所以表章天象之所在天
道之所在昭昭然溥之而橫乎四海者此也報
之隆非以其功之隆乎非矯誣以惑人也所以
發揚天象之所存天道之所存暴暴然推之而
及乎後世者此也報之崇非以其功之崇乎吁
郊則禮也報則義也先王豈無義而為虛禮也
哉抑論天何言哉道而已聖人何言哉亦天而
punctuated: 象也，聖人于以動而觀、靜而玩，萬事之紀立焉。星辰者，天垂之象也，聖人于以遠而探、近而索，四時之柄定焉。如日中星鳥、日永星火，東作南訛之事斯興。其他開一務、成一物，何者不本於天象以為之考中度衷乎？宵中星虛、日短星昴，西成朔易之事斯舉。其他創一法、立一制，何者不本諸天象以為之利用厚生乎？然作則雖始於聖人，垂象實原於天道。先王於是時維冬至，罄對越之忱，禋於南郊之丘，以冕則異於常也，以裘則異於常也；日用上辛，竭奏格之精，禋於南郊之兆，以車則異於常也，以旗則異於常也。是非徼福以自媚也，所以表章天象之所在、天道之所在，昭昭然溥之而橫乎四海者，此也。報之隆，非以其功之隆乎？非矯誣以惑人也，所以發揚天象之所存、天道之所存，暴暴然推之而及乎後世者，此也。報之崇，非以其功之崇乎？吁！郊則禮也，報則義也，先王豈無義而為虛禮也哉？抑論天何言哉？道而已。聖人何言哉？亦天而
translation_en: …are the signs displayed by Heaven. The sages observe them in activity and contemplate them in stillness, thereby establishing the ordering principles of all affairs. The stars and constellations are signs displayed by Heaven. The sages investigate them afar and examine them close at hand, thereby determining the governing principles of the four seasons. Thus, when day and night are equal and the Bird constellation appears, and when the days are longest and the Fire constellation appears, the work of spring cultivation in the east and summer transformation in the south begins. In undertaking any other task or bringing anything to completion, what does not take the celestial signs as its basis for examining and determining the proper mean? When night and day are equal and the Xu constellation appears, and when the days are shortest and the Mao constellation appears, the work of autumn completion in the west and winter renewal in the north is undertaken. In devising any other law or establishing any institution, what does not take the celestial signs as its basis for making resources useful and enriching the people's livelihood? Yet although the making of standards began with the sages, the display of celestial signs truly originates in the Way of Heaven. Accordingly, at the winter solstice the former kings poured out their sincerity in reverently responding to Heaven and offered pure sacrifice on the mound in the southern suburbs. Their ritual caps differed from ordinary ones, as did their fur robes. Choosing the first xin day, they exhausted their spiritual concentration in seeking to reach Heaven and offered pure sacrifice within the sacrificial precinct in the southern suburbs. Their carriages differed from ordinary ones, as did their banners. This was no seeking of blessings for their own gratification. It served to manifest where the celestial signs and the Way of Heaven reside: through this they were luminously spread throughout the Four Seas. Was not the magnificence of the requital due to the magnificence of Heaven's beneficence? Nor was this fabrication intended to delude people. It served to proclaim what the celestial signs and the Way of Heaven embody: through this they were radiantly extended to later generations. Was not the exalted character of the requital due to the exalted character of Heaven's beneficence? Ah! The suburban sacrifice is ritual; requital is its moral justification. Could the former kings have performed an empty ritual without moral justification? Moreover, what does Heaven say? It is simply the Way. What do the sages say? They too follow Heaven …

translation_en:
…the signs. Through these, the sages observed while active and contemplated while still, and thus established the ordering principles of all affairs. The stars are signs displayed by Heaven. Through these, the sages investigated what was distant and examined what was near, and thus determined the governing principles of the four seasons. For example, when day and night are equal and the Bird constellation appears, and when the days are longest and the Fire constellation appears, the tasks of spring cultivation and summer transformation begin. In undertaking any other task or bringing anything to completion, what did they not base upon celestial signs to examine and measure the proper mean? When night and day are equal and the Xu constellation appears, and when the days are shortest and the Mao constellation appears, the tasks of autumn harvesting and winter adjustment are undertaken. In devising any other law or establishing any institution, what did they not base upon celestial signs to make resources useful and enrich the people's livelihood?

Yet although the making of rules began with the sages, the display of signs truly originated in the Way of Heaven. Accordingly, at the winter solstice, the former kings exhausted their sincerity in reverently addressing Heaven and offered pure sacrifice upon the mound in the southern suburbs. Their ceremonial caps differed from those ordinarily worn, as did their dragon robes. Choosing the first xin day, they devoted their utmost spiritual concentration to presenting offerings and reaching Heaven, and offered pure sacrifice within the sacrificial precinct in the southern suburbs. Their carriages differed from those ordinarily used, as did their banners.

This was no attempt to seek blessings for their own gratification. It was the means of making manifest what the celestial signs and the Way of Heaven embodied, spreading this clearly throughout the Four Seas. Was not the grandeur of their requital due to the grandeur of Heaven's achievements? Nor was this fabrication intended to delude people. It was the means of proclaiming what the celestial signs and the Way of Heaven contained, extending this manifestly [?] to later generations. Was not the exalted character of their requital due to the exalted character of Heaven's achievements?

Ah! The suburban sacrifice is ritual; requital is righteousness. Could the former kings have performed empty ritual without righteousness? Yet what does Heaven say? It is simply the Way. What do the sages say? Likewise, only Heaven…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
已矣先王制禮以明天之道與社以報地之道
其義一也若夫所謂天書之降實所以誣天封
禪之議實所以褻天果可語先王之禮哉故曰
有國家者郊社之義不可不知
合生氣之和道五常之行
唐鎬
同考試官教諭林批題本好說人多失於浮
泛晚得此卷字字輕重皆有分曉平易中自是過人
當進之以與天下之士友焉
===
考試官教諭周批有理趣
考試官教諭方批善組織
賛化工之妙迪人心之天惟樂然也甚矣樂妙
天人之和也先王作樂欲以之為造化人心之用
焉樂其大矣乎樂記論聲音之應感及此蓋謂
本與末而兼該情與文而俱備先王之樂固已
盡善盡美矣將安用耶是故陽一動而為春為
夏生長由之而始隂一靜而為秋為冬收藏由
之而終此生育之氣也先王用樂以合焉寓諸
punctuated:
已矣。先王制禮以明天之道，與社以報地之道，其義一也。若夫所謂天書之降，實所以誣天；封禪之議，實所以褻天。果可語先王之禮哉？故曰：「有國家者，郊社之義不可不知。」

合生氣之和，道五常之行。
唐鎬

同考試官教諭林批：題本好說，人多失於浮泛。晚得此卷，字字輕重皆有分曉，平易中自是過人，當進之，以與天下之士友焉。
考試官教諭周批：有理趣。
考試官教諭方批：善組織。

賛化工之妙，迪人心之天，惟樂然也。甚矣，樂妙天人之和也！先王作樂，欲以之為造化人心之用焉。樂其大矣乎！《樂記》論聲音之應感及此，蓋謂本與末而兼該，情與文而俱備，先王之樂固已盡善盡美矣，將安用耶？是故陽一動而為春為夏，生長由之而始；隂一靜而為秋為冬，收藏由之而終。此生育之氣也，先王用樂以合焉，寓諸
translation_en:
…and nothing more. The former kings established rites to make manifest the Way of Heaven; these share the same underlying meaning as sacrifices at the altars of soil to requite the Way of Earth. As for the supposed descent of heavenly writings, this was truly a means of falsely attributing things to Heaven; proposals for the feng and shan sacrifices were truly a means of profaning Heaven. Can such things really be discussed as rites of the former kings? Thus it is said: “Those who govern states and households must understand the meaning of the suburban sacrifices and the sacrifices at the altars of soil.”

“Bringing into harmony the life-giving vital energies and guiding the practice of the Five Constant Virtues.”
Tang Hao

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: “The topic itself lends itself to discussion, but many candidates err by being superficial and vague. Late in the process I came upon this paper: the weight of every word is clearly judged. Within its plainness and ease it is naturally superior to others. Its author should be advanced, so that he may associate as a friend with the scholars of the realm.”
Comment by Examiner Zhou, Instructor: “It has the appeal of sound principle.”
Comment by Examiner Fang, Instructor: “Skillfully composed.”

To assist the wondrous workings of creation and bring forth what is Heaven-given in the human heart—only music can do this. How profound is music’s wondrous harmonizing of Heaven and humanity! The former kings created music intending to employ it in the workings of cosmic transformation and the human heart. How great music is! The Record of Music, in discussing how sounds respond to stimuli, reaches this point. Its meaning is that the music of the former kings embraced both root and branches and possessed both feeling and outward form; it was already perfectly good and perfectly beautiful. To what use, then, was it to be put? When yang moves, it produces spring and summer, initiating birth and growth; when yin rests, it produces autumn and winter, completing the cycle through gathering and storing. These are the vital energies that generate and nurture life. The former kings used music to bring them into harmony, embodying them in…

As for the supposed descent of celestial writings, this actually serves to misrepresent Heaven; proposals for the feng and shan sacrifices actually serve to profane Heaven. Can these truly be discussed as rites of the former kings? Thus it is said: “Those who possess a state or a ruling house must understand the meaning of the suburban sacrifice to Heaven and the sacrifice at the altar of the soil.”

“Bring into harmony the vital forces that engender life, and guide the practice of the five constant virtues.”
Tang Gao

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: The topic is inherently easy to discuss, but many fall into superficial generalities. I obtained this paper late in the process. The weight of every word is clearly judged; in its plainness and ease it naturally surpasses others. Its author should be advanced so that he may associate as a friend with the scholars of the realm.

Comment by Examiner Zhou, Instructor: It has philosophical interest.
Comment by Examiner Fang, Instructor: Skillfully organized.

To assist the wondrous workings of creation and bring forth what is Heaven-given in the human heart—music alone can do this. How profound is music’s wondrous harmonizing of Heaven and humanity! When the former kings created music, they intended it to serve the workings of creation and the human heart. How great music is! The Record of Music, in discussing how sounds respond to stimuli, reaches this point. Its meaning is surely that root and branch are both encompassed, and feeling and outward form are both fully present. The music of the former kings was already perfectly good and perfectly beautiful; to what use, then, would they put it? Thus, when yang becomes active, it produces spring and summer, initiating birth and growth; when yin becomes still, it produces autumn and winter, completing gathering and storing. These are the vital forces that engender and nurture life. The former kings used music to harmonize them, embodying them in…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
聲音者發而為播蕩之機使聖以産之仁以長
之一大化為之均調義以守之中以藏之一大
順為之洋溢發舒之内而有停畜嚴凝之中而
有絪縕不亢不𪘏所謂動四氣之和者此也吾
之氣順天地之氣豈有不順乎得乾之剛而為
仁為禮信亦存焉得坤之柔而為義為智信亦
賦焉此五常之行也先王用樂以道焉形諸節
奏者宣而為感召之方使發之也仁行之也中
一偽為之不容裁之也義處之也正一誠為之
===
無間嚴毅發於慈巽之餘和易形於直方之際
能讓能斷所謂著萬物之理者此也吾之心正
天下之心豈有不正乎吁化工以樂而和人心
以樂而善樂云樂云鐘鼓云乎哉嗟夫天下之
道二邪正之間而已故樂能賛天地之和亦能
傷天地之和能善民心之德亦能敗民心之德
此無他古樂與新樂和淫不同也如齊宣好世
俗之樂魏文好鄭衛之音皆先王之罪人也然
而當時之化不時則不生男女無辨則亂升非
punctuated:
聲音者，發而為播蕩之機，使聖以産之，仁以長之，一大化為之均調；義以守之，中以藏之，一大順為之洋溢。發舒之内而有停畜，嚴凝之中而有絪縕，不亢不𪘏，所謂動四氣之和者此也。吾之氣順，天地之氣豈有不順乎？得乾之剛而為仁為禮，信亦存焉；得坤之柔而為義為智，信亦賦焉。此五常之行也，先王用樂以道焉。形諸節奏者，宣而為感召之方，使發之也仁，行之也中，一偽為之不容；裁之也義，處之也正，一誠為之無間。嚴毅發於慈巽之餘，和易形於直方之際，能讓能斷，所謂著萬物之理者此也。吾之心正，天下之心豈有不正乎？吁！化工以樂而和，人心以樂而善。樂云樂云，鐘鼓云乎哉！
嗟夫！天下之道，二：邪正之間而已。故樂能賛天地之和，亦能傷天地之和；能善民心之德，亦能敗民心之德。此無他，古樂與新樂和淫不同也。如齊宣好世俗之樂，魏文好鄭衛之音，皆先王之罪人也。然而當時之化，不時則不生，男女無辨則亂，升非
translation_en:
…what is embodied in sound issues forth as the impulse that sets things in motion, so that sagacity brings them into being and benevolence nurtures them: the whole great process of transformation is thereby evenly regulated. Righteousness preserves them and centrality stores them away: a great accord thereby pervades all. Within unfolding and expansion there is restraint and accumulation; within stern consolidation there is the generative mingling of vital forces. There is neither excess nor deficiency [?]. This is what is meant by setting in motion the harmony of the vital forces of the four seasons. If my own vital force is in accord, how could the vital forces of Heaven and Earth fail to be in accord? From the firmness of Qian come benevolence and ritual propriety, with trustworthiness also present; from the yieldingness of Kun come righteousness and wisdom, with trustworthiness likewise bestowed. These are the workings of the Five Constant Virtues, which the former kings used music to guide. What takes form in rhythm is expressed as a means of eliciting a response, so that its arising is benevolent and its operation centered, admitting no falsity whatsoever; its regulation is righteous and its disposition correct, with a single sincerity uninterrupted throughout. Stern resolve emerges amid kindness and deference; harmony and ease appear amid uprightness and rectitude. There is the capacity both to yield and to decide. This is what is meant by making manifest the principles of the myriad things. If my own heart is upright, how could the hearts of all under Heaven fail to be upright? Ah! Through music, the work of creation becomes harmonious, and human hearts become good. When we speak of music, music, do we mean merely bells and drums?
Alas! The ways of the world are two: they lie simply between the deviant and the correct. Thus music can assist the harmony of Heaven and Earth, but it can also injure that harmony; it can improve the virtue of the people's hearts, but it can also corrupt that virtue. There is no other reason for this than the difference between ancient and new music, between harmony and licentiousness. Such rulers as King Xuan of Qi, who delighted in popular music, and Marquis Wen of Wei, who delighted in the sounds of Zheng and Wei, were all offenders against the former kings. Yet the transforming processes of that time—if they do not accord with the seasons, nothing grows; if men and women are not distinguished, disorder results—[?]…

Sageliness brings things into being, and benevolence nurtures them, so that the great transforming process is brought into balance; righteousness preserves them, and centrality stores them away, so that a great concord abounds. title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
樂也人也故君子當自脩以端作樂之本云
第貳場
論
臺諫以天下公議為主
陳汝謨
同考試官教諭楊批臺諫一論是昔之聖人見
得一人之聰明不足以盡天下之庶務故以耳目付臺諫而
臺諫主公議則四海九州之情自得其要領所謂簡要者
場中士子專以忠諫直作議論不知歸重在人主上殊
===
失立言本意惟此作有根據有發揚且下筆措詞脫去
陳腐氣習蓋蓄學有待之士也允宜錄出以示學者
考試官教諭周批論有抑揚開闔收拾在後
數語有識者之言也得士如此司校文者可以塞責矣
考試官教諭方批臺諫一論文勢滾滾從胸
中流出長江大河之才予其有之甚矣公議之難也異日
揚于
大廷子慎無忘斯言
人主設官以通天下之言本諸人心所同然者
punctuated:
樂也，人也。故君子當自脩，以端作樂之本云。

第貳場
論
臺諫以天下公議為主
陳汝謨

同考試官教諭楊批：臺諫一論，是昔之聖人見得一人之聰明不足以盡天下之庶務，故以耳目付臺諫。而臺諫主公議，則四海九州之情自得其要領，所謂簡要者。場中士子專以忠諫直作議論，不知歸重在人主上，殊失立言本意。惟此作有根據，有發揚，且下筆措詞脫去陳腐氣習，蓋蓄學有待之士也。允宜錄出，以示學者。

考試官教諭周批：論有抑揚開闔，收拾在後數語，有識者之言也。得士如此，司校文者可以塞責矣。

考試官教諭方批：臺諫一論，文勢滾滾，從胸中流出。長江大河之才，予其有之。甚矣，公議之難也！異日揚于大廷，子慎無忘斯言。

人主設官以通天下之言，本諸人心所同然者
translation_en:
…music, but people. Thus the gentleman should cultivate himself to set right the foundation for making music.

Second Session
Discourse
“The Censorate and Remonstrance Officials Take the Public Judgment of All under Heaven as Their Guiding Principle”
Chen Rumo

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: This discourse on the censorate and remonstrance officials concerns how the sages of old recognized that one person's powers of hearing and sight could not encompass all the myriad affairs of the realm. They therefore entrusted these officials with serving as their ears and eyes. When these officials take public judgment as their guiding principle, they naturally grasp the essentials of conditions throughout the Four Seas and Nine Provinces. This is what is meant by concision and attention to essentials. The candidates in the examination hall devoted their arguments exclusively to loyal remonstrance and forthrightness [?], failing to understand that the principal emphasis belongs on the ruler, and thus seriously missing the original intent of the proposition. This composition alone is well grounded and develops its meaning fully; moreover, its phrasing is free of stale expressions and habits. Its author is surely a scholar who has accumulated learning while awaiting his opportunity. It certainly deserves to be transcribed and shown to students.

Comment by Examiner Zhou, Instructor: The discourse has restraint and emphasis, opening and closure; it draws everything together in its final few phrases. These are the words of a discerning man. Having obtained a scholar such as this, those charged with evaluating compositions may consider their duty fulfilled.

Comment by Examiner Fang, Instructor: This discourse on the censorate and remonstrance officials pours forth from the writer's breast in a surging stream. I grant that he possesses a talent like the Yangzi and Yellow Rivers. How difficult public judgment is! When you are one day advanced at the imperial court, take care not to forget these words.

The ruler establishes offices to give the words of all under Heaven a channel of communication, grounding this in what human hearts alike acknowledge to be right…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
而已何也一人之心思不足以徧天下之耳目
一人之聰明不足以盡天下之見聞人主聰明
必有所寄然後任言責者得以盡難言之事而
廟廊之上日聞所不聞之言下無隱情上無壅
聽求天下無治豈可得哉否則堂下遠於百里
而跬步之外不勝其異議矣知乎此元城劉氏
所謂臺諫之論每以天下公議為主者可得而
論已請終其說日月經乎中天大可以被八荒
而小或不能入一室之下彼固無用此區區小
===
明也人主之知何以異是是故九州中處四海
外環君以眇然之躬深居九重之上一日萬幾
蓋亦繁且難哉將欲竭聰明營耳目包羅籠絡
使天下之衆必無所用其姦吾知其不能也昔
之聖人有見於此遂以耳目之任付之臺諫之
官蓋不自用其聰明而以臺諫為聰明不自私
其聞見而以臺諫為聞見不自役其耳目而以
臺諫為耳目非以小明不足恃而天下之情不
可不通也乎然官以諫為名則責任與百司異
punctuated: 而已。何也？一人之心思不足以徧天下之耳目，一人之聰明不足以盡天下之見聞。人主聰明必有所寄，然後任言責者得以盡難言之事，而廟廊之上日聞所不聞之言，下無隱情，上無壅聽，求天下無治，豈可得哉？否則堂下遠於百里，而跬步之外不勝其異議矣。知乎此，元城劉氏所謂臺諫之論每以天下公議為主者，可得而論已。請終其說：日月經乎中天，大可以被八荒，而小或不能入一室之下，彼固無用此區區小明也。人主之知何以異是？是故九州中處，四海外環，君以眇然之躬深居九重之上，一日萬幾，蓋亦繁且難哉！將欲竭聰明，營耳目，包羅籠絡，使天下之衆必無所用其姦，吾知其不能也。昔之聖人有見於此，遂以耳目之任付之臺諫之官。蓋不自用其聰明，而以臺諫為聰明；不自私其聞見，而以臺諫為聞見；不自役其耳目，而以臺諫為耳目。非以小明不足恃，而天下之情不可不通也乎？然官以諫為名，則責任與百司異
translation_en: …and nothing more. Why is this? One person’s thoughts cannot encompass everything seen and heard throughout the realm; one person’s discernment cannot exhaust all that is observed and learned throughout the realm. The ruler’s discernment must have something on which to rely. Only then can those charged with speaking out fully address matters that are difficult to voice, so that at court the ruler daily hears things previously unheard. When no circumstances below remain concealed and hearing above is unobstructed, could the realm possibly fail to be well governed? Otherwise, the space below the hall becomes more remote than a hundred li, and even a few steps away dissenting opinions are beyond counting. Once this is understood, we can discuss what Master Liu of Yuancheng meant when he said that the arguments of censors and remonstrance officials must always take the public judgment of the realm as their guiding principle. Allow me to complete the explanation. The sun and moon pass through the middle of the heavens: on the grand scale, their light can reach the eight remotest regions, yet on the small scale it may fail to penetrate beneath the roof of a single room. They assuredly have no need for such trifling illumination. How is the ruler’s knowledge any different? Thus, with the Nine Provinces situated within and the Four Seas encircling them, the ruler, a single slight figure, dwells deep within the ninefold palace. In a single day he faces ten thousand affairs: how numerous and difficult they are! Were he to exhaust his discernment, tax his eyes and ears, and encompass and control everything, so that none among the multitude in the realm could practice deceit, I know he could not succeed. The sage rulers of old perceived this and therefore entrusted the duty of serving as their eyes and ears to censors and remonstrance officials. They did not rely solely on their own discernment, but took that of these officials as their own; they did not treat their own observations as their exclusive resource, but took those of these officials as their own; they did not toil with their own eyes and ears, but made these officials their eyes and ears. Was this not because limited discernment could not be relied upon, while the true circumstances of the realm had to be communicated? Yet when an office takes its name from remonstrance, its responsibilities differ from those of the various other offices…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
而已何也一人之心思不足以徧天下之耳目
一人之聰明不足以盡天下之見聞人主聰明
必有所寄然後任言責者得以盡難言之事而
廟廊之上日聞所不聞之言下無隱情上無壅
聽求天下無治豈可得哉否則堂下遠於百里
而跬步之外不勝其異議矣知乎此元城劉氏
所謂臺諫之論每以天下公議為主者可得而
論已請終其說日月經乎中天大可以被八荒
而小或不能入一室之下彼固無用此區區小
===
明也人主之知何以異是是故九州中處四海
外環君以眇然之躬深居九重之上一日萬幾
蓋亦繁且難哉將欲竭聰明營耳目包羅籠絡
使天下之衆必無所用其姦吾知其不能也昔
之聖人有見於此遂以耳目之任付之臺諫之
官蓋不自用其聰明而以臺諫為聰明不自私
其聞見而以臺諫為聞見不自役其耳目而以
臺諫為耳目非以小明不足恃而天下之情不
可不通也乎然官以諫為名則責任與百司異
punctuated:
而已。何也？一人之心思不足以徧天下之耳目，一人之聰明不足以盡天下之見聞。人主聰明必有所寄，然後任言責者得以盡難言之事，而廟廊之上日聞所不聞之言，下無隱情，上無壅聽，求天下無治，豈可得哉？否則堂下遠於百里，而跬步之外不勝其異議矣。知乎此，元城劉氏所謂臺諫之論每以天下公議為主者，可得而論已。

請終其說。日月經乎中天，大可以被八荒，而小或不能入一室之下，彼固無用此區區小明也。人主之知何以異是？是故九州中處，四海外環，君以眇然之躬深居九重之上，一日萬幾，蓋亦繁且難哉！將欲竭聰明，營耳目，包羅籠絡，使天下之衆必無所用其姦，吾知其不能也。昔之聖人有見於此，遂以耳目之任付之臺諫之官。蓋不自用其聰明，而以臺諫為聰明；不自私其聞見，而以臺諫為聞見；不自役其耳目，而以臺諫為耳目。非以小明不足恃，而天下之情不可不通也乎？然官以諫為名，則責任與百司異，
translation_en:
…and that is all. Why is this? One person's thought cannot encompass the eyes and ears of all under Heaven; one person's discernment cannot exhaust all that is seen and heard throughout the realm. The ruler must entrust his powers of discernment to others. Only then can those charged with speaking out fully address matters difficult to speak of, and the court daily hear words it has never heard before. Below, no circumstances will remain concealed; above, nothing will obstruct the ruler's hearing. Could the realm then possibly remain without good government? Otherwise, the space below the audience hall will be more distant than a hundred li, and just a few steps away dissenting opinions will be beyond counting. Understanding this, we can discuss what Master Liu of Yuancheng meant when he said that the arguments of censors and remonstrance officials should always take the public judgment of all under Heaven as their guide.

Allow me to complete the explanation. The sun and moon traverse the heavens: on the largest scale, they can illuminate the eight farthest regions, yet on the smallest they may fail to reach the interior of a single room. They have no need of such petty, limited illumination. How is the ruler's understanding any different? Thus, with the Nine Provinces occupying the center and the Four Seas encircling them, the ruler, in his diminutive person, dwells secluded within the ninefold palace, attending to ten thousand affairs each day. How numerous and difficult these must be! If he intends to exhaust his discernment, strain his eyes and ears, and encompass and control everything, so that none among the multitude under Heaven can possibly practice deception, I know that he cannot succeed. The sage rulers of old perceived this and accordingly entrusted the function of eyes and ears to the censors and remonstrance officials. They did not rely on their own discernment, but took these officials as their discernment; they did not keep their knowledge of what was heard and seen to themselves, but took these officials as their sources of knowledge; they did not tax their own eyes and ears, but took these officials as their eyes and ears. Was this not because limited discernment cannot be relied upon, while the true circumstances of the realm must be communicated? Yet when an office takes remonstrance as its name, its responsibilities differ from those of the various administrative offices…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
何哉專一事者任一事之責而止守一職者懐
一職之責而止至於天下之得失生民之利害
社稷之大計惟所見聞而不係職司者獨臺諫
得言焉得其言而不言與言之而不盡其道奈
天下何奈社稷生民何於乎此所以必以公議
為主耶夫君之使臣臣之事君大公至正之道
而已矣大公至正之道非滅人言以求覆過取
小亮以私其君者之謂也以天下之公心言天
下之公議而已且公議何為而生歟蓋天理之
===
在人心者發為至情人情之不容已者形為公
議公議之同然者而為是是非非今執途之人
而與之為謀彼未必能也聚一邑之人而求之
當有所得矣邑之人豈必智於途人也哉論者
多則其見公耳又即邑之人而與之為謀雖有
中未必盡得也合一郡之人而求之所得者多
矣郡之人豈必智於邑人也哉論者愈多則其
見愈公耳而况天下同然之議其有不公者乎
故曰匹夫匹婦離而聽之雖愚合而聽之則神
punctuated:
何哉？專一事者，任一事之責而止；守一職者，懐一職之責而止。至於天下之得失、生民之利害、社稷之大計，惟所見聞而不係職司者，獨臺諫得言焉。得其言而不言，與言之而不盡其道，奈天下何？奈社稷生民何？於乎！此所以必以公議為主耶？夫君之使臣，臣之事君，大公至正之道而已矣。大公至正之道，非滅人言以求覆過、取小亮以私其君者之謂也，以天下之公心，言天下之公議而已。
且公議何為而生歟？蓋天理之在人心者，發為至情；人情之不容已者，形為公議；公議之同然者，而為是是非非。今執途之人而與之為謀，彼未必能也；聚一邑之人而求之，當有所得矣。邑之人豈必智於途人也哉？論者多，則其見公耳。又即邑之人而與之為謀，雖有中，未必盡得也；合一郡之人而求之，所得者多矣。郡之人豈必智於邑人也哉？論者愈多，則其見愈公耳。而况天下同然之議，其有不公者乎？故曰：「匹夫匹婦，離而聽之雖愚，合而聽之則神。」
translation_en:
…Why is this so? Those charged with a particular matter bear responsibility for that matter alone; those holding a particular office concern themselves with the responsibilities of that office alone. But as for successes and failures throughout the realm, benefits and harms to the people, and great plans for the state—matters that come to their notice but fall outside their assigned duties—only censors and remonstrance officials are entitled to speak about these. If, entitled to speak, they remain silent, or if they speak without fully fulfilling their duty, what will become of the realm? What will become of the state and its people? Alas! Is this why public judgment must be their guide? The ruler’s employment of his ministers and the ministers’ service to their ruler amount simply to the way of complete impartiality and utmost rectitude. This way does not mean suppressing others’ words to conceal faults, or cultivating petty fidelity to show partiality toward one’s ruler. It means simply expressing the public judgment of the realm with an impartial concern for the realm.
How, then, does public judgment arise? Heavenly principle within human hearts finds expression as the truest feelings; human feelings that cannot be restrained take shape as public judgment; and the shared convictions of public judgment establish what is right as right and what is wrong as wrong. Now, if you stop someone on the road and consult him about a plan, he may not be capable of advising you. But if you gather the people of a county and seek their counsel, you should gain something. Are the people of a county necessarily wiser than the person on the road? It is simply that when more people deliberate, their views become impartial. Again, if you consult the people of a county about a plan, although some of their advice may hit the mark, they may not grasp everything. If you bring together the people of a prefecture and seek their counsel, you will gain more. Are the people of a prefecture necessarily wiser than those of a county? It is simply that the more people deliberate, the more impartial their views become. How much more so with a judgment shared by the whole realm: could it be anything but impartial? Thus it is said: “Ordinary men and women, heard separately, may be foolish; heard together, they are divinely discerning.”

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
偏而聽之雖闇公而聽之則精臺諫舍此不足
以言職矣故公議之所是臺諫必是之君曰不
可臺諫曰可君曰不然臺諫曰然吾敢沽名哉
知有公議而已公議之所非臺諫必非之君曰
可從臺諫曰勿從君曰可聽臺諫曰勿聽吾敢
求勝哉知有公議而已甚至君非不尊也一或
枉道於天反道於地覆道於社稷無道於黎元
于焉持公議而必爭之宰執非不貴也一或悖
道於君逆道於人黷道於貨亂道於刑于焉據
===
公議而必折之他如事不可以輕入重罪不可
以生入死公議所不容也敢緘默乎法不可以
剝害於人財不可以擅加於賦公議所不愜也
敢淟涊乎情不可以委之於倖亂不可以啓之
於萌公議所必戮也又敢依違而不力乎夫然
則人主耳目之寄在衆賢而不在群小陟罰臧
否之柄在公朝而不在私門生民有欲可以言
通吾一人之身不出戶庭而四海九州物物無
遁情矣論而至是則知公議行而臺諫之職盡
punctuated:
偏而聽之雖闇，公而聽之則精。臺諫舍此，不足以言職矣。故公議之所是，臺諫必是之。君曰：「不可。」臺諫曰：「可。」君曰：「不然。」臺諫曰：「然。」吾敢沽名哉？知有公議而已。公議之所非，臺諫必非之。君曰：「可從。」臺諫曰：「勿從。」君曰：「可聽。」臺諫曰：「勿聽。」吾敢求勝哉？知有公議而已。甚至君非不尊也，一或枉道於天，反道於地，覆道於社稷，無道於黎元，于焉持公議而必爭之。宰執非不貴也，一或悖道於君，逆道於人，黷道於貨，亂道於刑，于焉據公議而必折之。
他如事不可以輕入重，罪不可以生入死，公議所不容也，敢緘默乎？法不可以剝害於人，財不可以擅加於賦，公議所不愜也，敢淟涊乎？情不可以委之於倖，亂不可以啓之於萌，公議所必戮也，又敢依違而不力乎？夫然則人主耳目之寄在衆賢，而不在群小；陟罰臧否之柄在公朝，而不在私門；生民有欲，可以言通。吾一人之身不出戶庭，而四海九州物物無遁情矣。論而至是，則知公議行而臺諫之職盡
translation_en:
…Listening one-sidedly brings obscurity; listening impartially brings clarity. If censors and remonstrance officials abandon this principle, they cannot be said to discharge their duties. Thus, whatever public judgment approves, they must approve. The ruler says, “It cannot be done”; they say, “It can.” The ruler says, “That is not so”; they say, “It is.” Would I dare seek fame? I recognize only public judgment. Whatever public judgment condemns, they must condemn. The ruler says, “This may be followed”; they say, “Do not follow it.” The ruler says, “This may be heeded”; they say, “Do not heed it.” Would I dare seek to prevail? I recognize only public judgment. Indeed, even though the ruler is supremely honored, if he should violate the Way in relation to Heaven, oppose it in relation to Earth, overturn it in relation to the altars of soil and grain, or act without it toward the common people, they must uphold public judgment and remonstrate with him. Though chief councillors hold exalted rank, if they should betray the Way in serving the ruler, oppose it in dealing with others, defile it through wealth, or disorder it in administering punishments, these officials must invoke public judgment and rebuke them.
Likewise, minor offenses must not be treated as grave ones, nor crimes that warrant sparing life be made capital offenses. Public judgment will not tolerate such things: dare they remain silent? Laws must not be used to exploit and harm the people, nor demands for revenue arbitrarily added to taxation. Public judgment finds such things unacceptable: dare they acquiesce ignobly? The handling of affairs must not be entrusted to favorites [?], nor disorder allowed to arise in its beginnings. Public judgment must condemn such things: dare they waver and fail to exert themselves? When this principle prevails, the ruler entrusts the role of his eyes and ears to the many worthy men, rather than to petty men; authority to promote and punish, commend and condemn, rests with the public court rather than private households; and when the people have wants, they can communicate them in words. “I, the ruler, need not leave my doors and courtyard, yet throughout the Four Seas and Nine Provinces nothing can conceal its true circumstances from me.” Having pursued the argument thus far, we know that when public judgment prevails, the duties of censors and remonstrance officials are fully discharged…

Even if listening with partiality leaves one benighted, listening impartially brings discernment. Without this, censors and remonstrance officials cannot be said to fulfill their duties. Thus, whatever public judgment approves, they must approve. If the ruler says, “It is unacceptable,” they say, “It is acceptable”; if the ruler says, “It is not so,” they say, “It is so.” Would we dare seek a reputation for ourselves? We recognize only public judgment. Whatever public judgment condemns, they must condemn. If the ruler says, “This may be followed,” they say, “Do not follow it”; if the ruler says, “This may be heeded,” they say, “Do not heed it.” Would we dare seek merely to prevail? We recognize only public judgment.

Indeed, it is not that the ruler is undeserving of reverence. But if he should violate the Way in relation to Heaven, act contrary to the Way in relation to Earth, overturn the Way in relation to the altars of soil and grain, or act without the Way toward the common people, then these officials must uphold public judgment and remonstrate with him. It is not that the chief councilors are undeserving of honor. But if they should flout the Way in serving the ruler, contravene it in dealing with others, sully it through wealth, or disrupt it in administering punishments, then these officials must invoke public judgment and rebuke them.

The circumstances of cases must not be left to favoritism [?], nor disorder allowed to arise in its first stirrings. Public judgment will assuredly condemn this: dare they again equivocate and fail to exert themselves?

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
臺諫賢而天下之治成古之聖人能通天下為
一身者其用此道歟雖然臺諫之設信善矣耳
目之責信專矣一或匪人則公議之場未必不
為假借私奉之地耳目之重未必不為報復恩

者公議之要也脩身以端取人之則者又為君

元祐八年五月七日，臣蘇軾、臣呂希哲、臣
translation_en:
…When the censors and remonstrance officials are worthy, good government throughout the realm is achieved. Was it by employing this way that the sages of antiquity could unite all under Heaven as a single body? Nevertheless, although establishing censors and remonstrance officials is certainly good, and their responsibility as the ruler’s ears and eyes is certainly their special charge, should an unsuitable person occupy such a post, the forum for public judgment may become a place for exploiting authority to serve private interests [?], and the weighty role of ears and eyes may become a means of repaying favors and settling grudges. Thus only broad-minded men will be impartial in accepting good counsel; only upright and trustworthy men will be correct in discussing affairs; only firm and principled men will be steadfast in maintaining their views; and only sincere and earnest men will be trustworthy in presenting counsel. Considered together, these points show that censors and remonstrance officials are essential to assisting government; public judgment is essential to their work; care in selecting men is essential to public judgment; and cultivating oneself so as to set right the standards for selecting men is, in turn, essential to being a ruler. Such is this discourse.

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
豐稷臣趙彥若臣范祖禹等誠惶誠恐稽
首頓首上言伏以昭德塞違獻納有裨於
至治篤信好古典刑端屬於老成惟善人
能受乎盡言而智者每視夫成事茲遇
〇〇〇〇
人惟求舊
法不喜新
隆大孝於
慈宮克篤周文視膳問安之至敬
===
紹徽猷於
列聖恒懷伯益滿損謙益之嘉謨
盛德過人
虛心無我罷青苗止雇役
明斷實出於
宸衷開言路起廢官正道方亨於今日臣等論
思是職未酬一得之愚採摘不嫌竊效三
篇之對伏見唐宰臣陸贄者言不離於道
德學可帝師論每切乎事情才幾王佐觀
punctuated: 豐稷、臣趙彥若、臣范祖禹等，誠惶誠恐，稽首頓首上言：伏以昭德塞違，獻納有裨於至治；篤信好古，典刑端屬於老成。惟善人能受乎盡言，而智者每視夫成事。茲遇〇〇〇〇，人惟求舊，法不喜新。隆大孝於慈宮，克篤周文視膳問安之至敬；紹徽猷於列聖，恒懷伯益滿損謙益之嘉謨。盛德過人，虛心無我。罷青苗，止雇役，明斷實出於宸衷；開言路，起廢官，正道方亨於今日。臣等論思是職，未酬一得之愚；採摘不嫌，竊效三篇之對。伏見唐宰臣陸贄者，言不離於道德，學可帝師；論每切乎事情，才幾王佐。觀
translation_en:
…Feng Ji, your servant Zhao Yanruo, your servant Fan Zuyu, and the others, in utmost fear and trepidation, bow their heads to the ground and repeatedly kowtow, submitting these words: We humbly consider that, in making virtue manifest and checking wrongdoing, the presentation of counsel contributes to perfect government; in holding firm to the Way and loving antiquity, the preservation of exemplary standards properly rests with mature and experienced men. Only the good can accept fully candid speech, and the wise always examine what has already been accomplished. Now we have the good fortune to encounter 〇〇〇〇 [four placeholder circles; referent uncertain], who seeks men of long service and takes no delight in novel laws.

You display profound filial devotion toward the palace of the imperial mother, faithfully practicing the utmost reverence shown by King Wen of Zhou in attending to his parent’s meals and inquiring after his well-being. You carry forward the excellent principles of the successive sage emperors, ever mindful of Bo Yi’s fine counsel that fullness brings loss and humility brings gain. Your abundant virtue surpasses that of others; your mind is receptive and free of self-regard. You abolished the Green Sprouts loan program and stopped the hired-service system: these discerning decisions truly issued from your imperial heart. You opened the channels for remonstrance and recalled dismissed officials: the proper Way now flourishes.

We, your servants, are charged with deliberation and reflection, yet have not repaid your favor with even a single useful insight from our humble understanding. If selecting excerpts is not deemed objectionable, we would venture to emulate the three responses to imperial questions. We humbly observe that Lu Zhi, a chief councilor of the Tang, never departed in his words from the Way and virtue; his learning qualified him to teach an emperor. His discussions always addressed the realities of affairs, and his ability approached that of a true royal counselor. Examining…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
其奏議一編之經略將與伊傅爭衡比諸
治安諸策之規模豈容董賈獨步下詔而
罪已萬方仰洗天浴日之功削號以改元
九廟仗旋乾轉坤之力他如用人聽言之
法足裨明目達聰之萬分治邊馭將之方
庶幾行遠升高之一助究其術雖不盡於
當世徵厥數似有待於
明時臣等鉛槧譾材草茅末學備員講讀慚
負
===
聖明憂時之念無窮而識則有限補
袞之心彌切而言或未能用資藥石之談藉
為曝芹之
獻上塵乙夜之
覽先求九弊之端儻置坐隅不止於言語文字
之益若能心得自兼夫堯舜禹湯之明伏
願
主善為師
聖學日躋於有極
punctuated:
其奏議一編之經略，將與伊傅爭衡；比諸治安諸策之規模，豈容董賈獨步？下詔而罪已，萬方仰洗天浴日之功；削號以改元，九廟仗旋乾轉坤之力。他如用人聽言之法，足裨明目達聰之萬分；治邊馭將之方，庶幾行遠升高之一助。究其術，雖不盡於當世；徵厥數，似有待於明時。
臣等鉛槧譾材，草茅末學，備員講讀，慚負聖明。憂時之念無窮，而識則有限；補袞之心彌切，而言或未能。用資藥石之談，藉為曝芹之獻，上塵乙夜之覽，先求九弊之端。儻置坐隅，不止於言語文字之益；若能心得，自兼夫堯舜禹湯之明。伏願主善為師，聖學日躋於有極。
translation_en:
…the plans for governance contained in this single collection of his memorials could rival those of Yi Yin and Fu Yue. Compared with the scope of the various policy proposals for securing peace and order, how could Dong Zhongshu and Jia Yi alone claim preeminence? When an edict acknowledging imperial fault was issued, all lands looked up to the achievement of cleansing Heaven and bathing the sun; when an imperial title was curtailed and the reign designation changed, the nine ancestral temples depended upon the power that turned Heaven and Earth around. Other matters, such as his methods of employing men and hearing advice, could contribute some tiny measure toward making imperial sight clear and hearing receptive. His methods of governing the frontiers and controlling generals might likewise offer some assistance in traveling far and ascending high. Examining his methods, we find that they were not fully put into effect in his own age; considering their destined course, it seems that they awaited an enlightened age.
We, your servants, are men of shallow talent, wielding stylus and writing tablet, humble scholars from the countryside. Filling places as lecturers and readers, we are ashamed to have fallen short of Your Majesty’s enlightened expectations. Our concern for the times is boundless, but our understanding is limited; our desire to mend the imperial robes—to remedy faults in government—is ever more earnest, yet our words may prove inadequate. We draw upon these medicinal words of counsel and present them as a rustic’s humble offering of sunshine and celery. We venture to trouble Your Majesty’s late-night reading, seeking first the sources of the nine abuses [?]. If this collection is kept beside your seat, its benefit will extend beyond words and writing; if its meaning is grasped in the heart, you will naturally unite in yourself the wisdom of Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang. We humbly pray that you take goodness as your teacher, and that your sagely learning advance daily toward the highest perfection.

…The statecraft embodied in this collected volume of memorials could rival that of Yi Yin and Fu Yue. When its scope is compared with the policy proposals for securing peace and order, how could Dong Zhongshu and Jia Yi be allowed to stand unrivaled? By issuing an edict acknowledging his own faults [the transcription is doubtful here: 已 for 己?], the ruler accomplished a cleansing of heaven and a bathing of the sun that all lands revered; by removing an honorific title and changing the reign designation, he exerted a power to turn heaven and earth around upon which the nine ancestral temples depended. We humbly pray that you take goodness as your teacher, and that your sagely learning advance daily toward the highest perfection…

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
以人爲鑑
皇圖天啓於無疆臣等無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屏營之至謹以所校奏議二十二卷隨
表上
進以
聞
第叁塲
策五道
===
第一問
陳汝謨
同考試官教諭楊批會典一書實備
國家一代之制周官法度大抵在是子生於百粤之鄉迺能條陳若是
固足以占用世之學益見
聖教漸摩無間遐邇也夫
考試官教諭周批
聖制策鋪叙甚善宜錄
考試官教諭方批會典一問欲觀諸士子
punctuated:
以人爲鑑，皇圖天啓於無疆。臣等無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹以所校奏議二十二卷隨表上進以聞。

第叁塲
策五道

正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
殿廷內政宗室等差則取諸
皇明祖訓孝慈錄凡約束臣民懲姦斥僭則取
諸
大誥大明令敎民榜兵制則取之軍法定律刑
辟則取之
大明律而內外執法之官則取諸
憲綱以為則至於百司庶務纖悉畢舉則一一
皆本於諸司職掌之所載也是故先之以
本
===
朝官職制度而大綱舉次之以事物儀文而
萬目張內列五軍六部以為居重馭輕之
本外列都司藩臬以為承宣防範之寄郡
縣之設提封萬里而各統于藩司衛所之
兵犬牙相參而各總于方鎮土官荒服屬
吏部者列于郡縣之次屬兵部者列于衛
所之次其體統名分蓋猶冠屨衣裳截然
而不可易者也至論其設官則文武雖並
置也而事皆歸于文職文職各有司也而
punctuated:
殿廷內政、宗室等差，則取諸《皇明祖訓》《孝慈錄》；凡約束臣民、懲姦斥僭，則取諸《大誥》《大明令》《敎民榜》；兵制則取之《軍法定律》；刑辟則取之《大明律》；而內外執法之官，則取諸《憲綱》以為則。至於百司庶務，纖悉畢舉，則一一皆本於《諸司職掌》之所載也。
是故先之以本朝官職制度，而大綱舉；次之以事物儀文，而萬目張。內列五軍、六部，以為居重馭輕之本；外列都司、藩臬，以為承宣防範之寄。郡縣之設，提封萬里，而各統于藩司；衛所之兵，犬牙相參，而各總于方鎮。土官荒服，屬吏部者列于郡縣之次，屬兵部者列于衛所之次。其體統名分，蓋猶冠屨衣裳，截然而不可易者也。至論其設官，則文武雖並置也，而事皆歸于文職；文職各有司也，而
translation_en:
…For the internal administration of the palace and the distinctions of rank within the imperial clan, it draws upon the Ancestral Injunctions of the August Ming (Huang Ming zuxun) and the Record of Filial Piety and Compassion (Xiaoci lu). For regulating subjects, punishing wrongdoing, and suppressing usurpations of privilege, it draws upon the Grand Pronouncements (Da gao), the Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming ling), and the Placard for Instructing the People (Jiaomin bang). For military organization, it draws upon the Established Statutes of Military Law (Junfa dinglü); for penal provisions, upon the Great Ming Code (Da Ming lü). For officials charged with enforcing the law at the capital and in the provinces, it takes the Censorial Regulations (Xian gang) as its standard. As for the manifold affairs of the government offices, comprehensively covered down to the smallest detail, every item is based upon what is recorded in the Duties of the Various Offices (Zhusi zhizhang).
Thus it first presents the official posts and institutions of our dynasty, setting out the main framework; it then presents administrative matters and ceremonial forms, unfolding their countless particulars. At the capital, it lists the Five Chief Military Commissions and the Six Ministries, which provide the basis for concentrating authority at the center and controlling the subordinate branches. In the provinces, it lists the Regional Military Commissions, Provincial Administration Commissions, and Provincial Surveillance Commissions, entrusted with transmitting and implementing imperial commands and maintaining safeguards. Prefectures and counties extend across a territory of ten thousand li, each under a Provincial Administration Commission; the troops of the guards and battalions interlock like a dog's teeth, each under a regional military command. Native officials in the distant frontier regions who fall under the Ministry of Personnel are listed after the prefectures and counties; those under the Ministry of War are listed after the guards and battalions. Their hierarchy and distinctions of status are like those between caps and shoes, upper and lower garments: sharply defined and not interchangeable. As for the establishment of official posts, although both civil and military officials are appointed, all affairs ultimately fall to the civil officials; and although the civil officials each have their own responsibilities, …

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
其成必關
內閣亦如周之六卿分職以倡九牧而冢宰
實掌邦治焉其大要合於周制者蓋在此
矣自周而降若漢之規模略定于三章唐
之儀式僅頒乎六典會要作於宋而光嶽
弗完經世紀於元而彝倫斯斁擬諸會典
不可同日而語明矣至於制異墳典者蓋
謂欲宜於今而不泥於古法殊紀傳者蓋
謂叙其事而不錄其名體有所重故事雖
===
微而必錄義可以訓故令雖寢而必書文
字之間盡用行移之語而不少潤飾者蓋
將使山谷田野之民易於誦習而便於遵
守然耳嗚呼天地之道所以博厚高明者
由其為物不貳我
祖宗之制作所以光前裕後者本乎
聖德之至誠自洪武以至于今百六十年間天
下一統而無敝者其本端在于此愚也不
〔識不知順帝之則而已蕪詞不足以復明〕
punctuated:
其成必關內閣，亦如周之六卿分職以倡九牧，而冢宰實掌邦治焉。其大要合於周制者，蓋在此矣。自周而降，若漢之規模略定于三章，唐之儀式僅頒乎《六典》，《會要》作於宋而光嶽弗完，《經世》紀於元而彝倫斯斁，擬諸《會典》，不可同日而語明矣。至於制異墳典者，蓋謂欲宜於今而不泥於古；法殊紀傳者，蓋謂叙其事而不錄其名。體有所重，故事雖微而必錄；義可以訓，故令雖寢而必書。文字之間，盡用行移之語而不少潤飾者，蓋將使山谷田野之民易於誦習而便於遵守，然耳。
嗚呼！天地之道所以博厚高明者，由其為物不貳。我祖宗之制作所以光前裕後者，本乎聖德之至誠。自洪武以至于今，百六十年間，天下一統而無敝者，其本端在于此。愚也不〔識不知，順帝之則而已。蕪詞不足以復明〕
translation_en:
…the completion of their work must involve the Grand Secretariat. This likewise resembles the Zhou arrangement, in which the Six Ministers divided their duties to lead the nine regional governors, while the Minister of State actually controlled the governance of the realm. Here, broadly speaking, lies its conformity with the Zhou system. After the Zhou, the framework of Han government was only roughly established in three articles of law; Tang institutional forms were promulgated merely in the Six Statutes (Liudian). The Collected Essentials (Huiyao) was compiled under the Song, yet the realm was territorially incomplete; the Ordering of the World (Jingshi) was recorded under the Yuan, yet the enduring moral relationships fell into disorder. Clearly, these cannot be spoken of in the same breath as the Collected Statutes (Huidian). As for its organization differing from the ancient canonical writings, this means that it seeks to suit the present without being bound by antiquity. Its method differing from that of annals and biographies means that it sets out administrative matters without recording the names of individuals. Because its form gives weight to these matters, even minor ones must be recorded; because their import can provide instruction, even orders no longer in effect must be written down. Throughout, it uses the language of official correspondence without the slightest embellishment, simply so that people in mountain valleys and rural fields may readily recite and study it and conveniently observe its provisions.
Ah! The Way of Heaven and Earth is broad and substantial, lofty and luminous, because its operation is undivided. The institutions established by our imperial ancestors illuminate what came before and enrich what follows because they are rooted in the utmost sincerity of their sagely virtue. From the Hongwu reign until now, during these one hundred and sixty years, the realm has remained united without deterioration: its fundamental basis lies precisely here. Ignorant as I am, I have no 〔understanding or knowledge, but merely follow the Supreme Lord’s standards. My crude words are insufficient to elucidate further…〕

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
間惟進教之幸甚
第二問
唐脩
同考試官教諭李批三場勻稱儒業一策上
下古今出入子史而評論明當末復重於所養非畧
然有識者不能如此且反覆辯論而筆力愈健凡近
者殆未可窺其際也表而出之用勵多士
考試官教諭周批東場所以觀士之閎博
此篇故實不遺而品藻精當且辭氣整贍若有未盡
===
其才者得士如此可稱賢科矣
考試官教諭方批策目淺易答者類見其
難此卷能答所問而文且典重豈亦有德者之言乎
對儒有鳴世盛而垂世遠必本諸中者深
而發乎外者宏矣德也功也言也所以鳴
世即所以垂世也是故德而不一非純德
也功而不正非崇功也言而不經非通言
也真儒無不純之德不崇之功不通之言
也上而兼焉次而各舉其盛焉後世猶有
punctuated:
間，惟進教之幸甚。
第二問
唐脩
同考試官教諭李批：三場勻稱。儒業一策，上下古今，出入子史，而評論明當；末復重於所養，非畧然有識者不能如此。且反覆辯論，而筆力愈健，凡近者殆未可窺其際也。表而出之，用勵多士。
考試官教諭周批：東場所以觀士之閎博。此篇故實不遺，而品藻精當，且辭氣整贍，若有未盡其才者。得士如此，可稱賢科矣。
考試官教諭方批：策目淺易，答者類見其難。此卷能答所問，而文且典重，豈亦有德者之言乎？
對：儒有鳴世盛而垂世遠，必本諸中者深，而發乎外者宏矣。德也，功也，言也，所以鳴世，即所以垂世也。是故德而不一，非純德也；功而不正，非崇功也；言而不經，非通言也。真儒無不純之德、不崇之功、不通之言也。上而兼焉，次而各舉其盛焉，後世猶有
translation_en:

Tang Xiu 唐脩

In this policy essay on the vocation of the Confucian scholar, he ranges through antiquity and the present, drawing freely on the philosophical masters and histories, with clear and fitting judgments. At the end he again emphasizes personal cultivation; such a treatment requires discernment [?]. Moreover, as he argues his points repeatedly from different angles, his writing grows ever more vigorous. Ordinary minds could scarcely glimpse the extent of his accomplishment. title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
問惟進教之幸甚
第二問
唐脩
同考試官教諭李批三場勻稱儒業一策上
下古今出入子史而評論明當末復重於所養非斷
然有識者不能如此且反覆辯難而筆力愈健凡近
者殆未可窺其際也表而出之用勵多士
考試官教諭周批東場所𠯁觀士之博聞
此篇故實不遺而品藻精當且辭氣整贍若有未盡
其才者得士如此可稱賢科矣
考試官教諭方批策目淺易答者類見其
難此卷能答所問而文且典重豈亦有德者之言乎
對儒有鳴世盛而垂世遠必本諸中者深
而發乎外者宏矣德也功也言也所以鳴
世即所以垂世也是故德而不一非純德
也功而不正非崇功也言而不經非通言
也真儒無不純之德不崇之功不通之言
也上而兼焉次而各舉其盛焉後世猶有
punctuated:
問，惟進教之，幸甚。

第二問
唐脩

同考試官教諭李批：三場勻稱，儒業一策，上下古今，出入子史，而評論明當。末復重於所養，非斷然有識者不能如此。且反覆辯難，而筆力愈健，凡近者殆未可窺其際也。表而出之，用勵多士。

考試官教諭周批：東場所𠯁觀士之博聞。此篇故實不遺，而品藻精當，且辭氣整贍，若有未盡其才者。得士如此，可稱賢科矣。

考試官教諭方批：策目淺易，答者類見其難。此卷能答所問，而文且典重，豈亦有德者之言乎？

title: 正德十四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
俟焉可也德不足而求之功功不足而求
之言抑淺爾噫天下微全人而君子有定
論矣夫德由身脩而大小分功由時建而
邪正形言由道考而醇駁判裒小而成大
去邪而就正袪駁而歸之醇吾以是觀其
養矣執事者于德于功于言皆屬舉而詢
焉愚有以知君子慨世之深意矣且忠如
屈原朱子以為過直如汲黯楊氏疑其褊
廉如時苗元世祖乃斥其矯約如王安石
===
蘇洵乃辯其姦蓋嘗眩於其迹至於自湛
其身與淮南寢謀之事夫然後知過之者
乃所以許之疑之者乃所以信之而似德
之害者固不容巳於辯且斥耳義如張巡
未免流俗之毁斷如寇準卒來孤注之喻
勇如李靖而東坡譏其失才如姚崇而頴
濱病其非蓋嘗惑於其說至於敘全天下
之半與親扶日轂之事夫然後知温公之
論一出於至公欽若之讒不失為士檢而
punctuated: 俟焉可也。德不足而求之功，功不足而求之言，抑淺爾。噫！天下微全人，而君子有定論矣。夫德由身脩而大小分，功由時建而邪正形，言由道考而醇駁判。裒小而成大，去邪而就正，袪駁而歸之醇，吾以是觀其養矣。執事者于德、于功、于言，皆屬舉而詢焉，愚有以知君子慨世之深意矣。且忠如屈原，朱子以為過；直如汲黯，楊氏疑其褊；廉如時苗，元世祖乃斥其矯；約如王安石，蘇洵乃辯其姦。蓋嘗眩於其迹，至於自湛其身與淮南寢謀之事，夫然後知過之者乃所以許之，疑之者乃所以信之，而似德之害者，固不容巳於辯且斥耳。義如張巡，未免流俗之毁；斷如寇準，卒來孤注之喻；勇如李靖，而東坡譏其失；才如姚崇，而頴濱病其非。蓋嘗惑於其說，至於敘全天下之半與親扶日轂之事，夫然後知温公之論一出於至公，欽若之讒不失為士檢，而
translation_en:
…it is permissible to await them. To seek achievement when virtue is insufficient, and words when achievement is insufficient, is, however, shallow. Alas! There are few wholly accomplished people in the world, yet the gentleman has settled judgments. Virtue arises from cultivating oneself, and thus its greater and lesser degrees are distinguished; achievements are established as circumstances allow, and thus their perversity or rectitude becomes apparent; words are examined against the Way, and thus their purity or admixture is determined. Gather what is small to make it great, discard perversity and approach rectitude, remove admixture and return to purity: by these means I assess a person's cultivation. You who preside over this examination have brought virtue, achievement, and words together and asked about them. I, in my ignorance, can thereby perceive the depth of your concern for the world.

Consider loyalty such as Qu Yuan's: Master Zhu judged it excessive; uprightness such as Ji An's: Master Yang suspected narrow-mindedness; incorruptibility such as Shi Miao's: Yuan Shizu denounced it as affectation; frugality such as Wang Anshi's: Su Xun exposed its deceit. Their outward conduct may at first have dazzled us. Only upon considering such events as Qu Yuan's drowning himself and the abandonment of Huainan's plot do we understand that finding fault with the former was a means of acknowledging him, and expressing doubt about the latter was a means of affirming him. As for the harm done by seeming virtue, one certainly cannot refrain from exposing and denouncing it.

Righteousness such as Zhang Xun's did not escape vulgar slander; decisiveness such as Kou Zhun's ultimately attracted the comparison to staking everything on a single throw; courage such as Li Jing's nevertheless drew Dongpo's criticism of his failings; talent such as Yao Chong's nevertheless drew Yingbin's censure of his faults. We may at first have been confused by these judgments. Only upon considering the account of preserving half the realm and the deed of personally supporting the sun's chariot—that is, the sovereign—do we understand that the judgment of the Duke of Wen, Sima Guang, proceeded entirely from the utmost impartiality, and that Qinruo's slander could still serve as a restraint upon men of service [?], and…

…it is permissible to await judgment. If virtue is insufficient, to look instead to achievements, and if achievements are insufficient, to look instead to words—this is shallow indeed. Alas! There are few perfect people in the world, yet the gentleman has settled standards of judgment. Virtue is cultivated in oneself, revealing its greater or lesser extent; achievements are established as circumstances allow, revealing their perversity or uprightness; words are examined against the Way, distinguishing the pure from the mixed.
